hints: Look up the two vanadium half equations in the Data Booklet and identify which has the more positive $E^{\ominus}$ value, as this will be the cathode.
walkthrough:
Pick out the two half cell potentials**
You have $\text{V}^{3+} + \text{e}^{-} \rightleftharpoons \text{V}^{2+}$ with $E^{\ominus} = -0.26\text{ V}$ and $\text{VO}_{2}^{+} + 2\text{H}^{+} + \text{e}^{-} \rightleftharpoons \text{VO}^{2+} + \text{H}_{2}\text{O}$ with $E^{\ominus} = +1.00\text{ V}$. The more positive one will gain electrons, so it is the cathode.

Apply E cathode minus E anode**
Use $$E^{\ominus}_{cell} = E^{\ominus}_{cathode} - E^{\ominus}_{anode}$$ Substitute: $$E^{\ominus}_{cell} = (+1.00) - (-0.26) = +1.26\text{ V}$$ A positive value confirms the reaction is feasible under standard conditions.

hints: Decide which vanadium species is oxidised and which is reduced by comparing the $E^{\ominus}$ values from (a)(i).
walkthrough:
Assign oxidation and reduction**
The $\text{VO}_{2}^{+}$ / $\text{VO}^{2+}$ couple at $+1.00\text{ V}$ is the oxidising agent, so $\text{VO}_{2}^{+}$ is reduced to $\text{VO}^{2+}$. The $\text{V}^{3+}$ / $\text{V}^{2+}$ couple at $-0.26\text{ V}$ is the reducing agent, so $\text{V}^{2+}$ is oxidised to $\text{V}^{3+}$.

Add the half equations**
Reduction: $\text{VO}_{2}^{+} + 2\text{H}^{+} + \text{e}^{-} \rightarrow \text{VO}^{2+} + \text{H}_{2}\text{O}$. Oxidation: $\text{V}^{2+} \rightarrow \text{V}^{3+} + \text{e}^{-}$. Electrons cancel one to one, giving $$\text{VO}_{2}^{+} + \text{V}^{2+} + 2\text{H}^{+} \rightarrow \text{VO}^{2+} + \text{V}^{3+} + \text{H}_{2}\text{O}$$ Check atoms, charge and $\text{H}^{+}$ balance.

hints: Recall that both half cells contain only ions in solution with no solid metal, so think about what type of electrode must dip into each beaker.
List which aqueous ions must be present together in the left beaker and which must be present together in the right beaker, including acid where $\text{H}^{+}$ appears in the half equation.
Remember the two external connections needed between beakers to allow ion flow and electron flow without mixing the solutions.
Think about how a voltmeter should be connected to measure the cell e.m.f. under zero current conditions.
walkthrough:
See why inert electrodes are essential**
Neither half cell has a vanadium metal rod to act as an electron conductor. Both couples are ion to ion, $\text{V}^{3+}$/$\text{V}^{2+}$ and $\text{VO}_{2}^{+}$/$\text{VO}^{2+}$. So you must dip an unreactive conductor into each solution to carry electrons to and from the external circuit. Use platinum or graphite in both beakers.

Place the correct chemicals in each beaker**
Put $\text{V}^{3+}(\text{aq})$ and $\text{V}^{2+}(\text{aq})$ together in one beaker. Put $\text{VO}_{2}^{+}(\text{aq})$, $\text{VO}^{2+}(\text{aq})$ and $\text{H}^{+}(\text{aq})$, for example dilute sulfuric acid, together in the other beaker. The acid is vital because $\text{H}^{+}$ appears in the $\text{VO}_{2}^{+}$/$\text{VO}^{2+}$ half equation.

Complete the circuit correctly**
Link the two solutions with a salt bridge, typically filter paper soaked in $\text{KNO}_{3}(\text{aq})$, to allow ion migration and maintain charge balance without mixing. Connect the two inert electrodes with wires through a high resistance voltmeter to measure the potential while drawing negligible current.

Label fully for the examiner**
Draw two labelled beakers, label all four ions plus acid, label both Pt or graphite electrodes, label the salt bridge and label the voltmeter. Clear labels earn each mark.

Final answer: Two beakers connected by a salt bridge, each containing an inert Pt or graphite electrode connected via wires to a voltmeter. One beaker contains $\text{V}^{3+}(\text{aq})$ + $\text{V}^{2+}(\text{aq})$; the other contains $\text{VO}_{2}^{+}(\text{aq})$ + $\text{VO}^{2+}(\text{aq})$ + $\text{H}^{+}(\text{aq})$ (acid).

hints: For each pair, write down the two relevant $E^{\ominus}$ values from the Data Booklet and calculate $E^{\ominus}_{cell} = E^{\ominus}_{cathode} - E^{\ominus}_{anode}$ using the more positive as cathode.
Recall that a positive $E^{\ominus}_{cell}$ means a reaction is feasible, while a negative or zero value means no reaction under standard conditions.
For the feasible case, balance electrons between the $\text{V}^{2+}$ oxidation and the $\text{Sn}^{4+}$ reduction to write the overall ionic equation.
walkthrough:
Test V2+ with Sn4+**
Relevant couples: $\text{Sn}^{4+} + 2\text{e}^{-} \rightleftharpoons \text{Sn}^{2+}$, $E^{\ominus} = +0.15\text{ V}$ and $\text{V}^{3+} + \text{e}^{-} \rightleftharpoons \text{V}^{2+}$, $E^{\ominus} = -0.26\text{ V}$. Tin is more positive, so $\text{Sn}^{4+}$ is reduced and $\text{V}^{2+}$ is oxidised. $$E^{\ominus}_{cell} = (+0.15) - (-0.26) = +0.41\text{ V}$$ Positive, so yes, reaction is feasible.

Write the balanced equation for the tin case**
Oxidation needs doubling to match the two electrons for tin: $2\text{V}^{2+} \rightarrow 2\text{V}^{3+} + 2\text{e}^{-}$. Reduction: $\text{Sn}^{4+} + 2\text{e}^{-} \rightarrow \text{Sn}^{2+}$. Add: $$2\text{V}^{2+} + \text{Sn}^{4+} \rightarrow 2\text{V}^{3+} + \text{Sn}^{2+}$$

Test VO2+ with Fe3+**
Relevant couples: $\text{Fe}^{3+} + \text{e}^{-} \rightleftharpoons \text{Fe}^{2+}$, $E^{\ominus} = +0.77\text{ V}$ and $\text{VO}_{2}^{+} + 2\text{H}^{+} + \text{e}^{-} \rightleftharpoons \text{VO}^{2+} + \text{H}_{2}\text{O}$, $E^{\ominus} = +1.00\text{ V}$. To oxidise $\text{VO}^{2+}$ to $\text{VO}_{2}^{+}$ you would need a stronger oxidising agent than $\text{Fe}^{3+}$, but $+0.77$ is less positive than $+1.00$. $E^{\ominus}_{cell}$ for $\text{VO}^{2+} + \text{Fe}^{3+}$ would be negative, so no reaction occurs.

Final answer: $\text{V}^{2+}(\text{aq})$ and $\text{Sn}^{4+}(\text{aq})$: yes, reaction occurs. $E^{\ominus}_{cell} = (+0.15) - (-0.26) = +0.41\text{ V}$. $2\text{V}^{2+} + \text{Sn}^{4+} \rightarrow 2\text{V}^{3+} + \text{Sn}^{2+}$
$\text{VO}^{2+}(\text{aq})$ and $\text{Fe}^{3+}(\text{aq})$: no reaction.
